title: Erysichthon. Fames
titleEn: The Groaning Oak and the Breath of Hunger — Metamorphoses VIII.725–884
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The river of Calydon, propped on one elbow, tells Theseus — who wants to hear more of the gods' marvels — first of Proteus' many shapes and then of Erysichthon, who fells Ceres' sacred oak and is punished with a Hunger fetched from the frozen edge of Scythia. He eats through his inheritance, sells his shape-changing daughter to one master after another, and at last begins on his own body; the speaker closes with his own limited power of change and the horn he no longer has.

advisory.lede: These lines contain the rape of Erysichthon's daughter by Neptune, spoken of in her own words, and her flight from a man who has bought her.
advisory.more: At VIII.847–854 the daughter, sold by her starving father, stretches her hands over the sea and prays to the god who took her virginity by force to save her from the master pursuing her along the shore; Neptune answers by changing her shape, and her father then sells her again and again to new masters. Ovid gives the rape itself in two words, “raptae virginitatis”, as a fact already accomplished on which the prayer depends. The text is presented unaltered, and the translations and notes render what the Latin says at the force it says it.

sentences.t:
Desierat cunctosque et res et moverat auctor,
Thesea praecipue.
sentences.l: He had ceased, and both the matter and the teller had moved them all — Theseus above all.
sentences.i: He had finished, and both the tale and the man telling it had stirred them all — Theseus most of all.
sentences.n: The doubled subject “et res et auctor”, the story and its teller, shares the one verb “moverat”. The pluperfect “Desierat” closes off the previous narrative before the new speaker begins; the one who answers at 727 is the river of Calydon, that is Achelous.

sentences.t:
Quem facta audire volentem
mira deum, innixus cubito Calydonius amnis
talibus adloquitur:
sentences.l: And him, wanting to hear the wondrous deeds of the gods, the Calydonian river, leaning on his elbow, addresses with words such as these:
sentences.i: And since he was eager to hear more of the gods' marvels, the river of Calydon, propped on one elbow, addressed him so:
sentences.n: “Quem” is a connecting relative — “and him” — the ordinary Latin way of opening a sentence with a pronoun that points back to the last one. “deum” is the contracted genitive plural for “deorum”, everywhere in verse; “innixus cubito” puts the speaker on a banqueting couch.

sentences.t:
“Sunt, o fortissime, quorum
forma semel mota est et in hoc renovamine mansit,
sentences.l: “There are those, o bravest one, whose shape has been moved once and has stayed in this renewal,
sentences.i: “There are some, bravest of men, whose form was altered once and has remained in that new shape,
sentences.n: “Sunt ... quorum” leaves its antecedent unexpressed — “there are (those) of whom” — as regularly with “sunt qui”. The verbs “mota est” and “mansit” are indicative, so these are definite people rather than a supposed class; “renovamine” is an abstract noun in -men, a formation the poets take freely.

sentences.t:
sunt, quibus in plures ius est transire figuras,
ut tibi, complexi terram maris incola, Proteu.
sentences.l: there are those to whom there is the right to pass into more shapes than one — as to you, dweller of the sea that embraces the land, Proteus.
sentences.i: and there are those who have the right to pass through many shapes — as you do, Proteus, who live in the sea that clasps the earth.
sentences.n: “quibus ius est” is a dative of possession carrying an infinitive: “for whom there is the right to pass across into”. “complexi ... maris” is a genitive with “incola”, and the participle belongs to the deponent “complector”, so it is active in sense — the sea does the embracing. “Proteu” is a Greek vocative.

sentences.t: Nam modo te iuvenem, modo te videre leonem;
sentences.l: For at one moment they saw you a young man, at another they saw you a lion;
sentences.i: For men have seen you now a youth, now a lion;
sentences.n: “videre” is the poetic third-plural perfect, equal to “viderunt” — you will meet this ending constantly (compare “duxere” at 746 and “circuiere” at 748). The subject is the indefinite “people”, and “te iuvenem” is a double accusative, object plus predicate.

sentences.t:
nunc violentus aper, nunc, quem tetigisse timerent,
anguis eras, modo te faciebant cornua taurum.
sentences.l: now you were a violent boar, now a snake which they would fear to have touched; at another time horns made you a bull.
sentences.i: now you were a raging boar, now a serpent men would have dreaded to touch; and at times horns made you a bull.
sentences.n: “quem tetigisse timerent” is a relative clause of characteristic, with the subjunctive: “the sort of snake one would be afraid to have touched”. The perfect infinitive after a verb of fearing is normal Latin and need not be rendered as a past in English.

sentences.t: Saepe lapis poteras, arbor quoque saepe videri;
sentences.l: Often you could be seen a stone, often also a tree;
sentences.i: Often you could show as a stone, and often as a tree;
sentences.n: “poteras ... videri” is pulled to the two ends of the line, “you could be seen (as)”. Here “quoque” is the plain adverb “also” — but watch the word: the same letters are often “quō-que”, “and by which”, the ablative of the relative with “-que”, as at 866.

sentences.t:
interdum, faciem liquidarum imitatus aquarum,
flumen eras, interdum undis contrarius ignis.
sentences.l: sometimes, having imitated the appearance of flowing waters, you were a river; sometimes fire, opposite to the waves.
sentences.i: sometimes, taking on the look of running water, you were a river; sometimes fire, the very opposite of water.
sentences.n: “imitatus” is the perfect participle of the deponent “imitor” and is active in sense — “having imitated”, not “having been imitated”. “contrarius” takes the dative “undis”, “set against the waves”.

sentences.t:
Nec minus Autolyci coniunx, Erysichthone nata,
iuris habet.
sentences.l: Nor has the wife of Autolycus, born of Erysichthon, less of that right.
sentences.i: No less of that power belongs to the wife of Autolycus, Erysichthon's daughter.
sentences.n: “minus iuris” is a partitive genitive, “less of right”, picking up the “ius” of 730. “Erysichthone nata” is an ablative of origin, the regular Latin for “daughter of”. She is given no personal name anywhere in these lines, only her father, her husband and, at 872, a patronymic.

sentences.t:
Pater huius erat, qui numina divum
sperneret et nullos aris adoleret odores.
sentences.l: Her father was one who would scorn the divine powers of the gods and burn no incense on the altars.
sentences.i: Her father was a man who despised the powers of the gods and burned no offering on their altars.
sentences.n: “sperneret” and “adoleret” are subjunctives in a relative clause of characteristic — “the sort of man who ...”, not a statement of two occasions. “divum” is again the contracted genitive plural (“divorum”), and “adolere odores” is the technical phrase for burning incense in sacrifice.

sentences.t:
Ille etiam Cereale nemus violasse securi
dicitur et lucos ferro temerasse vetustos.
sentences.l: He is even said to have violated Ceres' grove with the axe and to have profaned the ancient woods with iron.
sentences.i: They say too that he violated Ceres' grove with the axe and profaned the ancient groves with the blade.
sentences.n: “dicitur” takes a nominative with the infinitive — “he is said to have ...” — where English may also turn it into “they say that he ...”. “violasse” and “temerasse” are syncopated perfect infinitives for “violavisse”, “temeravisse”; “ferro”, “with iron”, is the standard metonymy for a blade.

sentences.t:
Stabat in his ingens annoso robore quercus,
una nemus;
sentences.l: There stood among them a huge oak with aged timber, one tree a grove;
sentences.i: Among them stood a huge oak, its timber old with years — one tree that was a whole grove;
sentences.n: “annoso robore” is an ablative of description, “of aged oak-wood”. “una nemus” is a bold apposition, the single tree simply called a grove. “robur” means both the oak's hard timber and, by extension, the tree itself, as at 753 and 770.

sentences.t:
vittae mediam memoresque tabellae
sertaque cingebant, voti argumenta potentis.
sentences.l: fillets and remembering tablets and garlands encircled its middle, proofs of a prayer that had power.
sentences.i: Woollen fillets, tablets that kept the memory, and wreaths ringed its trunk — evidence of a prayer that had prevailed.
sentences.n: “mediam” is an adjective used as a noun, “its middle part”, the object of “cingebant”; the tree is feminine, “quercus”. “memores tabellae” are inscribed votive tablets, which remember the vow on the giver's behalf. Magnus prints “voti ... potentis”, the prayer that prevailed; some editions print “potentum”, making them the tokens of the vow of those who prevailed.

sentences.t: Saepe sub hac dryades festas duxere choreas,
sentences.l: Often beneath it the dryads led their festal dances,
sentences.n: “duxere” is once more the short perfect for “duxerunt” (compare “videre” at 732), and “choreas ducere” is the set phrase for leading a ring-dance. These dryads are the nymphs of this very wood, which is why they take the loss personally at 777.

sentences.t:
saepe etiam manibus nexis ex ordine trunci
circuiere modum,
sentences.l: often too, with hands linked in a row, they went around the compass of the trunk,
sentences.i: often, too, they joined hands in a line and ringed the measure of its trunk,
sentences.n: “manibus nexis” is an ablative absolute — a self-contained “with hands linked” where English wants a clause. “modum trunci” is the trunk's compass, the thing their linked arms had to span; “circuiere” is the poetic perfect for “circuierunt”.

sentences.t:
mensuraque roboris ulnas
quinque ter implebat.
sentences.l: and the measure of the oak filled out five ells three times over.
sentences.i: and the oak's girth came to fifteen ells.
sentences.n: “ulnas quinque ter”, “five ells three times”, is the poets' way of saying fifteen without a flat numeral. The “ulna” is a measure taken from the arm, which is why the dancers' linked arms have just been described.

sentences.t:
Nec non et cetera tantum
silva sub hac, silva quantum fuit herba sub omni.
sentences.l: And what is more, the rest of the wood was as much beneath this tree as the grass was beneath the whole wood.
sentences.i: And the rest of the forest stood as low beneath this one tree as grass stands beneath a whole forest.
sentences.n: “Nec non et” is a double negative used as an emphatic connective, “and what is more”. The proportion runs on “tantum ... quantum”, “as much ... as”, with “fuit” doing duty in both halves: the oak dwarfs the wood exactly as the wood dwarfs the grass.

sentences.l: Yet the son of Triopas did not for that reason hold his iron back from those things, and orders his servants to cut down the sacred oak;
sentences.i: Even so, the son of Triopas did not keep his blade from them for all that, and orders his slaves to fell the sacred oak;
sentences.n: “illa” is an ablative of separation with “abstinuit” — he kept the iron away from “those things”, the fillets and tablets just described. “Triopeius” is a patronymic: Erysichthon, son of Triopas. Note the shift from the perfect “abstinuit” to the historic present “iubet”, which brings the scene forward as the crime begins.

sentences.t:
et ut iussos cunctari vidit, ab uno
edidit haec rapta sceleratus verba securi:
sentences.l: and when he saw the men he had ordered hesitating, the criminal, the axe having been snatched from one of them, uttered these words:
sentences.i: and when he saw the men he had ordered hanging back, the criminal snatched the axe from one of them and uttered these words:
sentences.n: “rapta ... securi” is an ablative absolute pulled apart, with “sceleratus verba” standing inside it; “securis” has ablative “securi”. “sceleratus”, “the criminal”, is the narrator's own word for him, not a character's — the poem convicts him before he opens his mouth.

sentences.t:
“Non dilecta deae solum, sed et ipsa licebit
sit dea, iam tanget frondente cacumine terram.”
sentences.l: “Not only beloved of the goddess — granted that she be the goddess herself — she will touch the earth this instant with her leafy top.”
sentences.i: “Not merely the goddess's darling — let her be the goddess herself, if she likes — she will be touching the ground with her leafy crown this instant.”
sentences.n: “licebit” with the subjunctive “sit” is concessive, “granted that she be”, and the whole clause is thrown into the sentence like a parenthesis. The threat is in the plain future indicative “tanget”, and “frondente cacumine” keeps the living crown in view at the moment he promises to bring it down.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et obliquos dum telum librat in ictus,
contremuit gemitumque dedit Deoia quercus:
sentences.l: He spoke; and while he was poising his weapon for slanting strokes, Deo's oak shuddered and gave a groan:
sentences.i: He spoke; and as he balanced the blade for the slanting blow, the oak of Deo shuddered and let out a groan:
sentences.n: “dum” with the present indicative “librat” is regularly rendered by an English past, the present marking that the action is still going on when the main verb lands. “Deoia” is the adjective from Deo, a Greek name of Ceres, and marks the tree as hers; “obliquos in ictus” is the woodman's angled cut.

sentences.t:
et pariter frondes, pariter pallescere glandes
coepere ac longi pallorem ducere rami.
sentences.l: and equally the leaves, equally the acorns began to grow pale, and the long branches to draw on pallor.
sentences.i: and leaf and acorn alike began to blanch, and the long boughs to draw a pallor over themselves.
sentences.n: “coepere” is the short perfect for “coeperunt” and governs both infinitives, while the doubled “pariter ... pariter” spreads one verb over two subjects. The pallor is the colour of a body dying: Ovid treats the tree as flesh from the first stroke, and Pallor will turn up as a resident of Hunger's country at 790.

sentences.t:
Cuius ut in trunco fecit manus impia vulnus,
haud aliter fluxit discusso cortice sanguis,
sentences.l: And when the impious hand made a wound in its trunk, blood flowed out, the bark having been struck away, in no other manner
sentences.i: And when that unholy hand made a wound in the trunk, blood ran from the shattered bark in just the way
sentences.n: “Cuius” is a connecting relative — “and ... in its trunk” — the genitive depending on “trunco”. “discusso cortice” is an ablative absolute, “the bark having been struck apart”; “haud aliter ... quam”, “in no other way than”, opens the simile that the next unit completes, a favourite Ovidian way in through a negative.

sentences.t:
quam solet, ante aras ingens ubi victima taurus
concidit, abrupta cruor e cervice profundi.
sentences.l: than blood is accustomed to be poured out from the severed neck, when before the altars the huge victim, a bull, falls.
sentences.i: the blood pours from the severed neck when a great bull falls as a victim before the altars.
sentences.n: “profundi” is a present passive infinitive depending on “solet”, and its subject is “cruor” — “blood is accustomed to be poured out”. “abrupta ... cervice” is an ablative of source with “cruor e” wedged inside it. The comparison turns the felling into a sacrifice performed backwards: “victima” is the technical word for the beast offered, and here the offering is the goddess's own tree.

sentences.t:
Obstipuere omnes, aliquisque ex omnibus audet
deterrere nefas saevamque inhibere bipennem.
sentences.l: They were all struck dumb, and someone out of them all dares to deter the abomination and to check the savage double-axe.
sentences.i: They were all struck dumb, and one man out of the whole company dares to try to stop the abomination and hold back the cruel axe.
sentences.n: “Obstipuere” is again the short perfect, and the tense then jumps to the historic present “audet”, which holds the one man's courage at the moment of it. “nefas” is not merely a crime but what religion forbids, the unspeakable thing; the abstract noun stands for the deed itself.

sentences.t:
Adspicit hunc “mentis” que “piae cape praemia!” dixit
Thessalus,
sentences.l: The Thessalian looks at him and “take,” he said, “the rewards of a dutiful mind!”
sentences.i: The Thessalian looked at him: “Take the reward of your piety!” he said.
sentences.n: The quotation is broken open after its first word so that the connective “-que” of “mentisque piae” can stand outside the quotation marks — the printed page follows Ovid's word order rather than tidying it, and “dixit” comes after the whole speech. “Thessalus”, the man of Thessaly, is Erysichthon named by his country as he was named by his father at 751; the “reward” he offers is the blow that follows.

sentences.t:
inque virum convertit ab arbore ferrum
detruncatque caput repetitaque robora caedit,
sentences.l: and he turns the iron away from the tree against the man, and lops off his head, and cuts at the oak taken up again,
sentences.i: and he turned the blade from the tree upon the man, struck off his head, and went back to hacking at the oak,
sentences.n: “ab arbore ... in virum” frames the change of target with two prepositions, away from the one and against the other. “repetita ... robora” is a participle doing the work of an English adverb — the oak “resumed”, that is, he returns to it; “detruncat” is literally “lops the trunk of”, the felling metaphor carried over to a man.

sentences.t: redditus et medio sonus est de robore talis:
sentences.l: and such a sound was returned from the middle of the oak:
sentences.i: and from the heart of the oak there came back a voice like this:
sentences.n: “redditus ... est” is a perfect passive split around the centre of the line, and “medio robore” is once more the adjective standing for a part, “from the oak's middle”. “reddere” is the word for an answer given back: the tree replies to the axe.

sentences.t: “Nympha sub hoc ego sum Cereri gratissima ligno,
sentences.l: “I am a nymph beneath this wood, most dear to Ceres,
sentences.i: “I am a nymph inside this timber, dearest of all to Ceres,
sentences.n: “sub hoc ... ligno” is wrapped around “ego sum”, so that the pronoun sits inside the wood exactly as the nymph does. “Cereri” is a dative with “gratissima”, the regular construction with adjectives of pleasing.

sentences.t:
quae tibi factorum poenas instare tuorum
vaticinor moriens, nostri solacia leti.”
sentences.l: who, dying, prophesy to you that the penalties of your deeds stand close at hand — the consolations of my death.”
sentences.i: and dying I foretell to you that punishment for what you have done is at hand — the one comfort of my death.”
sentences.n: “quae ... vaticinor” is a relative clause with a first-person verb agreeing with the speaker, “I, who prophesy”, an idiom English usually flattens. “poenas instare” is accusative and infinitive after the verb of speaking; “nostri” is the poetic plural for “my”, and “nostri solacia leti” stands in apposition to the prophecy — the punishment coming to him is the comfort of her dying.

sentences.t:
Persequitur scelus ille suum, labefactaque tandem
ictibus innumeris adductaque funibus arbor
corruit et multam prostravit pondere silvam.
sentences.l: He pursues his crime through to the end; and the tree, at last shaken loose by countless blows and drawn down by ropes, fell and laid low much of the wood with its weight.
sentences.i: He carried his crime through; and the tree, loosened at last by countless blows and hauled down with ropes, crashed and flattened a great stretch of the wood beneath its weight.
sentences.n: “Persequitur scelus suum” is grimly exact — he “follows his crime through”, the verb of seeing a task out. “labefacta” and “adducta” are two perfect participles agreeing with “arbor” and separated by the line-end, so the sentence itself totters before the verb “corruit” arrives.

sentences.t:
Attonitae dryades damno nemorumque suoque,
omnes germanae, Cererem cum vestibus atris
maerentes adeunt poenamque Erysichthonis orant.
sentences.l: The dryads, thunderstruck at the loss both of the groves and their own, all of them sisters, go mourning to Ceres in black garments and beg for Erysichthon's punishment.
sentences.i: The dryads, stunned by the loss — the woods' and their own — all of them sisters, went in mourning black to Ceres and begged for Erysichthon's punishment.
sentences.n: “damno” is an ablative of cause, with “nemorum” the genitive depending on it and “suoque” a second ablative agreeing with “damno” understood again — the loss of the woods, and their own loss. “poenam Erysichthonis” is an objective genitive — punishment inflicted on him, not by him; “cum vestibus atris” is the black of Roman mourning, transferred to woodland nymphs.

sentences.t:
Adnuit his capitisque sui pulcherrima motu
concussit gravidis oneratos messibus agros.
sentences.l: She nodded to them, and, most beautiful, with a motion of her own head she shook the fields loaded with heavy harvests.
sentences.i: She nodded assent, and with that motion of her head the loveliest of goddesses shook the fields weighed down with their heavy crops.
sentences.n: “Adnuit” is literally “nodded towards”, the physical gesture that is also the standing word for granting a prayer, and the nod is then given a visible consequence. “pulcherrima” is a superlative used as a noun for Ceres herself; “oneratos ... messibus” keeps the harvest full in view at the exact moment famine is decreed.

sentences.t:
Moliturque genus poenae miserabile, si non
ille suis esset nulli miserabilis actis,
pestifera lacerare Fame.
sentences.l: And she contrives a kind of punishment to be pitied — were he not, by his own deeds, pitiable to nobody — to tear him with pestilent Hunger.
sentences.i: And she devised a punishment that would deserve pity, if his own acts had not put him beyond anyone's pity: to tear him apart with plague-bearing Hunger.
sentences.n: “si non ... esset” is a present contrary-to-fact condition dropped in as a parenthesis: the punishment would be pitiable, but he is not. The infinitive “lacerare” explains what the “genus poenae” is; “Fame” is the ablative of “fames”, and the capital in the edition shows that Hunger is already a person here.

sentences.t:
Quae quatenus ipsi
non adeunda deae est (neque enim Cereremque Famemque
fata coire sinunt),
sentences.l: And since she must not be approached by the goddess herself (for the fates do not allow Ceres and Hunger to come together),
sentences.i: And since the goddess herself may not go to her — for fate does not permit Ceres and Hunger to meet —
sentences.n: “adeunda ... est” is a gerundive of obligation and “ipsi deae” is its dative of agent: “must not be gone to by the goddess herself”. “Quae” is a connecting relative picking up Hunger from the line before, and the doubled “-que ... -que” of “Cereremque Famemque” is an epic mannerism yoking in grammar the two names that the fates will not let meet.

sentences.t:
montani numinis unam
talibus agrestem compellat oreada dictis:
sentences.l: she addresses one of the mountain divinity, a country oread, with such words as these:
sentences.i: she called on one of the mountain spirits, a rustic oread, with words like these:
sentences.n: “unam ... oreada” is split across the line-end, with “montani numinis” a partitive genitive, “one of the mountain godhead”. “oreada” is a Greek accusative singular in -a, kept in its Greek shape; “compellat” takes the person in the accusative and the words in the ablative.

sentences.t:
“Est locus extremis Scythiae glacialis in oris,
triste solum, sterilis, sine fruge, sine arbore tellus;
sentences.l: “There is a place at the furthest edges of icy Scythia, a dismal soil, a barren land, without corn, without a tree;
sentences.i: “There is a place on the outermost borders of frozen Scythia, a bleak soil, a barren country, with no grain and no tree;
sentences.n: “Est locus” is the standard epic formula for opening a set description of a place. The appositions then pile up without connectives, and “sterilis” is feminine, agreeing with “tellus” at the line's end; the repeated “sine ... sine” defines the country entirely by what it has not got.

sentences.t:
Frigus iners illic habitant Pallorque Tremorque
et ieiuna Fames.
sentences.l: There dwell sluggish Cold and Pallor and Trembling and fasting Hunger.
sentences.i: There live numbing Cold, and Pallor, and Shivering, and starving Hunger.
sentences.n: “habitant” is plural for a list of subjects that begins with the singular “Frigus” — the verb agrees with the whole company. These are personified abstractions, capitalised by the edition; “iners” is “inactive, sluggish”, and the epithet passes to what the cold works — a cold that makes everything sluggish, which is why the literal keeps “sluggish” and the idiomatic reads “numbing”; “ieiuna” is the word for an empty, fasting stomach, so Hunger is named by the state she inflicts.

sentences.t:
Ea se in praecordia condat
sacrilegi scelerata iube;
sentences.l: Order that she bury herself in the accursed vitals of the sacrilegious man;
sentences.i: Order her to bury herself in the accursed vitals of that sacrilegious man;
sentences.n: “iube” governs the subjunctive “condat” with no “ut”, the jussive standing on its own. “scelerata” may be taken as neuter plural with “praecordia”, the accursed vitals, as here, or as nominative feminine with the subject, making Hunger herself the accursed one; the word order permits either. “praecordia” is the region below the heart, seat of feeling as much as of digestion.

sentences.t:
nec copia rerum
vincat eam, superetque meas certamine vires.
sentences.l: and let no abundance of things overcome her, nor beat my strength in the contest.
sentences.i: and let no plenty of provisions defeat her, or outmatch my own strength in the trial.
sentences.n: Two jussive subjunctives, “vincat” and “superet”, both negated by the single “nec”. “certamine” makes the punishment a contest between plenty and hunger — the goddess of the grain harvest arranging that grain shall lose.

sentences.t:
Neve viae spatium te terreat, accipe currus,
accipe quos frenis alte moderere dracones.”
sentences.l: And lest the length of the road frighten you, take my chariot, take the dragons for you to steer on high with the reins.”
sentences.i: And so the length of the road may not daunt you, take my chariot; take these dragons, to guide aloft with the reins.”
sentences.n: “Neve ... terreat” is a negative purpose clause continuing the imperative, “and so that it may not frighten you”. “quos ... moderere” is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive, and “moderere” is the alternative second-person ending for “moderēris”, from the deponent “moderor”; the winged serpents are Ceres' own team throughout her cult.

sentences.t:
Et dedit. Illa dato subvecta per aera curru
devenit in Scythiam rigidique cacumine montis
(Caucason appellant) serpentum colla levavit
sentences.l: And she gave them. She, carried up through the air by the given chariot, came down into Scythia and on the summit of a rigid mountain (they call it Caucasus) lifted the serpents' necks free,
sentences.i: And she gave them. Borne up through the air in the chariot she had been given, the nymph came down into Scythia, and on the peak of a stiff mountain — Caucasus, men call it — she freed the serpents' necks,
sentences.n: “dato ... curru” is an ablative of means, noun and participle pulled to the ends of the phrase with “subvecta per aera” inside them, “by the chariot that had been given”. “Caucason” is a Greek accusative in -on, object of “appellant”, whose subject is the indefinite “they”; “colla levavit” is the technical action of unyoking, lifting the necks out of the harness.

sentences.t:
quaesitamque Famem lapidoso vidit in agro
unguibus et raras vellentem dentibus herbas.
sentences.l: and she saw the Hunger she had sought in a stony field, tearing at scanty grasses with nails and with teeth.
sentences.i: and there in a stony field she saw the Hunger she had come to find, pulling at the sparse grass with nails and teeth.
sentences.n: “quaesitam” is a perfect participle doing the work of a whole clause, “whom she had come looking for”. “vellentem” agrees with “Famem” and governs the two ablatives of instrument, “unguibus” and “dentibus”, which the line holds apart; “raras herbas” are grasses growing thinly — the only food this ground affords, and Hunger is eating it.

sentences.t:
Hirtus erat crinis, cava lumina, pallor in ore,
labra incana situ, scabrae rubigine fauces,
sentences.l: Her hair was shaggy, her eyes hollow, pallor on her face, her lips white with mould, her throat rough with rust,
sentences.i: Her hair was matted, her eyes sunken, her face all pallor, her lips gone white with mould, her throat rough with rust,
sentences.n: One verb “erat” serves the whole catalogue, which then drops even that and runs on in bare nouns and adjectives — the asyndeton is the portrait's method. “lumina”, “lights”, is the ordinary poetic word for eyes; “situ” and “rubigine” are ablatives of cause, the words for mould on neglected things and rust on iron, here applied to a body.

sentences.t:
dura cutis, per quam spectari viscera possent;
ossa sub incurvis exstabant arida lumbis,
sentences.l: her skin hard, through which the inward parts could be looked at; her dry bones stood out beneath her curved loins,
sentences.i: her skin hard, and through it the inner parts could be seen; the dry bones stood out under the bowed loins,
sentences.n: “spectari ... possent” is a passive infinitive under the subjunctive of a relative clause of characteristic — skin of a kind through which what lay under it could be seen. “viscera” covers everything beneath the skin, flesh as well as organs; the edition's spelling “exstabant” is kept exactly as printed.

sentences.t:
ventris erat pro ventre locus, pendere putares
pectus et a spinae tantummodo crate teneri.
sentences.l: in place of a belly there was the place of a belly; you would have thought her breast hung, and was held only by the wickerwork of the spine.
sentences.i: where the belly should have been there was only the space for one; you would have thought her chest hung loose, held up by nothing but the lattice of her spine.
sentences.n: The line turns on its own repetition: the belly has been replaced by the mere room a belly takes up. “putares” is a potential subjunctive addressed to nobody in particular, “you would have thought”, and it governs both infinitives “pendere” and “teneri”; “crate” is the word for wickerwork or hurdles, ribs and backbone seen as a frame.

sentences.t:
Auxerat articulos macies, genuumque tumebat
orbis, et inmodico prodibant tubere tali.
sentences.l: Thinness had enlarged her joints, and the round of her knees was swollen, and her ankles projected with an immoderate knob.
sentences.i: Wasting had made her joints look bigger; the disc of her knees was swollen, and her ankle-bones stood out in a great lump.
sentences.n: The paradox is grammatically exact: “macies”, the wasting, is the subject of “auxerat”, “had increased” — the joints look larger because everything around them has gone. “tali” is nominative plural, the ankle-bones, and “inmodico ... tubere” is an ablative of manner in the edition's unassimilated spelling.

sentences.t:
Hanc procul ut vidit (neque enim est accedere iuxta
ausa), refert mandata deae:
sentences.l: When she saw her from a distance (for she did not dare to approach close by), she reports the goddess's orders:
sentences.i: When she caught sight of her from far off — for she did not dare come near — she delivered the goddess's commands;
sentences.n: “est ... ausa” is the perfect of the semi-deponent “audeo”, passive in form and active in meaning, split around the line-end. “Hanc” stands first as the emphatic object of “vidit”, and the parenthesis explains why the messenger delivers her errand from where she stands.

sentences.t:
paulumque morata,
quamquam aberat longe, quamquam modo venerat illuc,
sentences.l: and having delayed only a little, although she was far away, although she had only just come there,
sentences.i: and after lingering only a moment — though she was still far off, though she had only just arrived —
sentences.n: “morata” is the perfect participle of the deponent “moror” and is active, “having delayed”. The doubled “quamquam ... quamquam” takes the indicative, as concessive “quamquam” regularly does; both clauses exist to sharpen the next line's point, that this contagion needs neither nearness nor time.

sentences.t:
visa tamen sensisse famem retroque dracones
egit in Haemoniam, versis sublimis habenis.
sentences.l: she nevertheless seemed to have felt hunger, and drove the dragons back into Haemonia, aloft, with the reins turned.
sentences.i: she nevertheless seemed to feel hunger, and turned the reins and drove her dragons back aloft to Haemonia.
sentences.n: “visa” needs “est” supplied from the sense, “she seemed”, with the perfect infinitive “sensisse”; the second witness prints the “est” that Magnus leaves to be understood. Here “famem” is the common noun, hunger the sensation, against the personified “Fames” all round it; “versis ... habenis” is an ablative absolute, and Haemonia is Thessaly, Erysichthon's country.

sentences.t:
Dicta Fames Cereris, quamvis contraria semper
illius est operi, peragit.
sentences.l: Hunger carries out the words of Ceres, although she is always contrary to her work.
sentences.i: Hunger carried out Ceres' instructions, opposed though she always is to what Ceres does.
sentences.n: “quamvis” here takes the indicative “est”, as it often does in verse where prose would want the subjunctive (contrast “quamvis ... esset” at 852). “contraria” governs the dative “operi”, and “illius” is the genitive of “ille” pointing back to Ceres; “peragit” is “carries through to the end”, the same completeness as “persequitur” at 774.

sentences.t:
Perque aera vento
ad iussam delata domum est
sentences.l: and through the air she was carried by the wind to the ordered house,
sentences.i: and the wind carried her through the air to the house she had been ordered to,
sentences.n: “delata ... est” is a perfect passive split by “domum”, with “vento” an ablative of means. “iussam ... domum” transfers the participle from the person to the thing: the house is called “ordered” because she was ordered to it.

sentences.t:
et protinus intrat
sacrilegi thalamos altoque sopore solutum
(noctis enim tempus) geminis amplectitur ulnis:
sentences.l: and at once she enters the bedchamber of the sacrilegious man and embraces him, loosened by deep sleep (for it was the time of night), with twin arms:
sentences.i: and at once she entered the sacrilegious man's chamber and, since it was night and he lay slack in deep sleep, took him in both her arms.
sentences.n: “solutum”, “loosened”, is the object of “amplectitur”, the man himself left to be supplied — sleep is regularly said to loose the limbs. “altoque sopore” is an ablative of cause; the parenthesis “noctis enim tempus” has no verb at all, as often in explanatory asides, and “geminis ulnis” brings back the word used for the oak's measurement at 748.

sentences.t:
seque viro inspirat faucesque et pectus et ora
adflat et in vacuis spargit ieiunia venis.
sentences.l: and she breathes herself into the man, and blows upon his throat and breast and mouth, and scatters fastings through his empty veins.
sentences.i: and she breathed herself into him, blowing upon throat and breast and mouth, and sowed starvation through his empty veins.
sentences.n: “se inspirat viro” is reflexive with a dative — she breathes herself into him, so that the goddess is the infection. The three objects strung on “-que ... et ... et” follow the breath over each in turn; “ieiunia” is plural, fasting made into something that can be strewn, and “spargit” is the verb for sowing seed, in a poem where the grain belongs to Ceres.

sentences.t:
Functaque mandato fecundum deserit orbem
inque domos inopes adsueta revertitur antra.
sentences.l: And having discharged her commission she leaves the fruitful world and returns into her destitute dwellings, her accustomed caves.
sentences.i: Her charge discharged, she left the fertile world and went back to her destitute home, the caves she was used to.
sentences.n: “Functa” is the perfect participle of the deponent “fungor”, which takes the ablative, “having performed her commission”. “domos inopes” and “adsueta antra” are one place named twice, apposition doing the work of a relative clause; “fecundum orbem”, the fertile world, is precisely what her own home is not.

sentences.t:
Lenis adhuc somnus placidis Erysichthona pennis
mulcebat:
sentences.l: Gentle sleep was still soothing Erysichthon with peaceful wings:
sentences.i: Gentle sleep was still stroking Erysichthon with its quiet wings:
sentences.n: “Erysichthona” is a Greek accusative in -a. The imperfect “mulcebat” holds the last calm moment open, and “adhuc”, “still”, warns the reader that it is about to end; sleep with wings is the standard shape of the god Somnus.

sentences.t:
petit ille dapes sub imagine somni
oraque vana movet dentemque in dente fatigat
sentences.l: he seeks feasts under the appearance of sleep, and moves his empty mouth, and wears tooth on tooth,
sentences.i: he reached for banquets in the semblance of his dream, worked his mouth on nothing, and ground tooth against tooth,
sentences.n: “sub imagine somni” is “under the image of sleep”, the Latin way of saying “in a dream”. “dentem in dente fatigat” sets the same noun in two cases side by side, accusative against ablative, so that the grinding is in the grammar; “vana ora” means empty in the sense of having nothing in them.

sentences.t:
exercetque cibo delusum guttur inani
proque epulis tenues nequiquam devorat auras.
sentences.l: and he works his gullet, cheated by empty food, and in place of banquets swallows thin airs to no purpose.
sentences.i: and he worked a throat cheated with food that was not there, and instead of a feast swallowed thin air for nothing.
sentences.n: “cibo ... inani”, the empty food, is wrapped around “delusum guttur”, the cheated throat, each adjective standing clear of its own noun — Ovid's favourite interlocked order. “pro epulis” is “in exchange for”, and “nequiquam”, “to no purpose”, is the word that fixes the whole punishment.

sentences.t:
Ut vero est expulsa quies, furit ardor edendi
perque avidas fauces incensaque viscera regnat.
sentences.l: But when rest had been driven out, the burning to eat rages, and reigns through his greedy throat and his kindled vitals.
sentences.i: But once sleep was driven off, the craving to eat raged, and ruled through his greedy throat and burning vitals.
sentences.n: “edendi” is a gerund in the genitive depending on “ardor”, “the burning of eating”. “regnat” is a startling choice: the appetite does not merely burn but reigns, the verb of a king, in a body that has become its kingdom; “incensa viscera” starts the fire that will be made an explicit simile at 837.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, quod pontus, quod terra, quod educat aer,
poscit
sentences.l: There is no delay: what the sea, what the land, what the air brings forth, he demands,
sentences.i: There was no pause: whatever sea, land or air brings forth, he demanded,
sentences.n: “Nec mora” is a verbless formula, “and no delay”, used to hurry a narrative forward. The three “quod” clauses share the single verb “educat”, which is written out only in the third, and the indicative is right because he asks for everything that really exists, not for a supposed class of things.

sentences.t:
et adpositis queritur ieiunia mensis
inque epulis epulas quaerit;
sentences.l: and with the tables set beside him he complains of fastings, and among banquets seeks banquets;
sentences.i: and with the tables spread before him he complained of starving, and in the middle of a feast looked for a feast;
sentences.n: “adpositis ... mensis” is an ablative absolute, “the tables having been set beside him”. “in epulis epulas” puts the same noun twice in two cases, the trick already used with “dentem in dente” at 825; the repetition is at once the joke and the horror.

sentences.t:
quodque urbibus esse
quodque satis poterat populo, non sufficit uni,
sentences.l: and what could be enough for cities, and what could be enough for a whole people, is not enough for one man,
sentences.i: and what could have satisfied whole cities, what could have satisfied a nation, is not enough for one man,
sentences.n: “esse ... satis” is split across the line-end, with “satis” serving both “quod” clauses and “poterat” to be supplied in the first. “urbibus”, “populo” and “uni” are all datives with “satis”, and the three of them shrink from cities to a people to a single man, while the verb changes from “poterat” to the present “sufficit” as the reckoning reaches him.

sentences.t: plusque cupit, quo plura suam demittit in alvum.
sentences.l: and he desires more, by however much the more he sends down into his own belly.
sentences.i: and the more he sends down into his belly, the more he wants.
sentences.n: “quo” with a comparative answers an unexpressed “eo”: “by how much more ... by so much the more”. Latin puts the craving first and the eating that feeds it second, which is why the literal here reads back to front against natural English.

sentences.t:
Utque fretum recipit de tota flumina terra
nec satiatur aquis peregrinosque ebibit amnes,
sentences.l: And as the sea takes in the rivers from the whole earth and is not sated with waters and drinks up foreign streams,
sentences.i: And as the sea receives the rivers of the whole earth and is never sated with water, but drinks up streams from far away,
sentences.n: “Ut ... utque ... sic” opens a double simile, the sea and then fire, which does not close until “sic” at 840 — keep that in view or the sentence loses its footing. “satiatur” is passive, “is not sated”, and in these lines it is the sea that gets the word and never Erysichthon; “peregrinos amnes” are rivers born in other lands, and the speaker telling this is himself a river.

sentences.t:
utque rapax ignis non umquam alimenta recusat
innumerasque faces cremat et, quo copia maior
est data, plura petit turbaque voracior ipsa est:
sentences.l: and as greedy fire never refuses nourishment and burns countless torches, and, by how much the greater supply has been given it, seeks more, and is itself the more devouring for the heap:
sentences.i: and as ravening fire never refuses fuel, burns up countless brands, and the more it is given the more it seeks, growing greedier from the very mass of it:
sentences.n: “quo ... maior ... plura” is the same correlative pair as at 834, comparative answering comparative. “turba” is an ablative of cause, “because of the crowd of things”, and “voracior ipsa est” makes the fire itself the devourer — the word the whole passage has been building toward. Magnus prints “faces”, torches; some editions print “trabes”, beams of timber.

sentences.t:
sic epulas omnes Erysichthonis ora profani
accipiunt poscuntque simul.
sentences.l: so the mouth of profane Erysichthon takes in all banquets and demands them at the same time.
sentences.i: so the mouth of unhallowed Erysichthon takes in every feast and calls for more in the same breath.
sentences.n: “ora” is the poetic plural for a single mouth and is the subject of the two plural verbs. “profani” means standing outside what is sacred, the same charge as “sacrilegi” at 792 and 817, kept alive as a fixed epithet; “accipiunt poscuntque simul” is the point of both similes at once — the taking and the demanding are one act.

sentences.t:
Cibus omnis in illo
causa cibi est, semperque locus fit inanis edendo.
sentences.l: In him all food is a cause of food, and the place is always made empty by eating.
sentences.i: In him every food is the cause of more food, and eating is what keeps the space empty.
sentences.n: “in illo” is “in his case”, the ablative of the person in whom something holds good. “edendo” is a gerund in the ablative of means, “by eating”; the sentence is framed as a general law rather than a description, and it is the paradox the rest of the episode carries out.

sentences.t:
Iamque fame patrias altaque voragine ventris
attenuarat opes,
sentences.l: And now by hunger and by the deep whirlpool of his belly he had worn away his father's wealth,
sentences.i: By now his hunger and the deep gulf of his belly had worn his inherited wealth thin,
sentences.n: “attenuarat” is the syncopated pluperfect for “attenuaverat”, “had worn away”. “patrias opes” is the estate that came down from his father, and the adjective is doing more work than “his own” would. Magnus reads “altaque voragine ventris”, the deep whirlpool of his belly; some editions print “altique ... ventris”, the whirlpool of his deep belly.

sentences.t:
sed inattenuata manebat
tum quoque dira fames, implacataeque vigebat
flamma gulae.
sentences.l: but even then the dread hunger remained unworn-away, and the flame of his unappeased gullet was in full vigour.
sentences.i: but even then the terrible hunger stayed undiminished, and the flame of his unappeasable throat burned as strong as ever.
sentences.n: “inattenuata” is formed straight against “attenuarat” in the line before: the wealth is worn away, the hunger is not. “implacatae ... gulae” is a genitive with “flamma”, and “gula” is the blunt word for the gullet used of greed; “vigebat” is the verb of health and vigour, given here to the disease instead of the man.

sentences.t:
Tandem, demisso in viscera censu,
filia restabat, non illo digna parente.
sentences.l: At last, his rated property having been sent down into his vitals, a daughter remained, not worthy of that father.
sentences.i: At last, with his whole estate sent down into his belly, there remained a daughter — who deserved a better father than that one.
sentences.n: “demisso ... censu” is an ablative absolute, and “census” is the formal word for a man's assessed property, the whole Roman valuation swallowed. “digna” governs the ablative “illo parente”; the litotes “non digna” says by understatement what the poem declines to say outright.

sentences.t: Hanc quoque vendit inops. Dominum generosa recusat
sentences.l: Her too, being without means, he sells. Nobly born, she refuses a master,
sentences.i: Her too he sold, beggared as he was. Nobly born, she refused a master,
sentences.n: “quoque” here is the plain adverb “too”, adding the daughter to the property already sold. “inops” and “generosa” are both nominative adjectives doing the work of clauses — “now that he was destitute”, “well-born as she was” — and the two are set against each other across the sentence: his poverty, her birth.

sentences.t: et vicina suas tendens super aequora palmas
sentences.l: and stretching her own palms out over the neighbouring waters
sentences.i: and stretching her hands out over the sea that lay close by
sentences.n: “tendens ... palmas” is the gesture of prayer, the hands held out towards the god addressed — here the sea, because the god she is about to call on is in it. “vicina ... aequora” is accusative after “super”, and the participle keeps the whole line waiting for the verb of speaking, which does not arrive until 851.

sentences.t:
“eripe me domino; qui raptae praemia nobis
virginitatis habes” ait.
sentences.l: “snatch me away from a master — you who hold the reward of my virginity, taken by force,” she says.
sentences.i: “Snatch me from a master — you who hold the prize of the virginity you took from me by force,” she said.
sentences.n: “eripe ... domino” uses the dative of the person from whom something is snatched, and the verb shares its root with “raptae” in the next clause: she asks the god who seized her to seize her again, this time to save her. “raptae ... virginitatis” is a genitive with “praemia”, and “nobis” is the poetic plural for “me”. The god she is addressing is not named until the end of the following line.

sentences.t: Haec Neptunus habebat.
sentences.l: These things Neptune had.
sentences.i: It was Neptune who held them.
sentences.n: The sentence is deliberately flat and deliberately late: “haec”, “these things”, is the “praemia” of the line before, and the name arrives only at the end, so that the rapist and the rescuer are identified as one person in three words. “habebat” is imperfect, the state that has gone on since.

sentences.t:
Qui prece non spreta, quamvis modo visa sequenti
esset ero, formamque novat vultumque virilem
induit et cultus piscem capientibus aptos.
sentences.l: And he, her prayer not having been scorned, although she had just been seen by her master as he followed, makes her form new and puts on her a man's face and the dress suited to those catching fish.
sentences.i: And he did not scorn her prayer, though her master, close behind, had just that moment caught sight of her: he made her form new, put a man's face upon her and the gear that suits men catching fish.
sentences.n: “prece non spreta” is an ablative absolute with a litotes inside it — “the prayer not having been scorned” rather than “granted”. “quamvis ... esset” takes the subjunctive here, against the indicative “est” with “quamvis” at 814; “sequenti ero” is a dative with the passive “visa esset”, “had been seen by”, or more literally “had shown herself to”, her master as he came after her. “piscem capientibus” is a participle used as a noun in the dative, the poem avoiding the flat word for fishermen.

sentences.t:
Hanc dominus spectans “o qui pendentia parvo
aera cibo celas, moderator harundinis,” inquit
sentences.l: Her master, looking at her, said, “O you who hide the hanging bronze with a little food, manager of the rod,
sentences.i: Her master, watching her, said: “You there, who hide the dangling bronze under a scrap of bait, you handler of the rod,
sentences.n: “pendentia ... aera” is neuter plural, the bronze hooks, and it is split apart by “parvo ... cibo”, the bait — the word order sets the hook inside the bait exactly as the sense does. “qui ... celas” is a relative clause with a second-person verb, the regular Latin way of addressing a stranger by what he is doing; “moderator harundinis” is a formal vocative, “manager of the reed”.

sentences.t:
“sic mare compositum, sic sit tibi piscis in unda
credulus et nullos, nisi fixus, sentiat hamos:
sentences.l: so may the sea be settled for you, so may the fish in the water be trusting to you and feel no hooks except once it is stuck fast:
sentences.i: may the sea lie calm for you, may the fish in the water trust you and never feel a hook until it is caught on one:
sentences.n: “sic ... sic” opens a prayer-bargain — “on this condition may things go well with you” — whose condition arrives at “dic ubi sit”. “sit” serves both “compositum” and “credulus” across the line-end, and “nisi fixus” is a compressed conditional, the participle standing in for “unless it has been hooked”.

sentences.t:
quae modo cum vili turbatis veste capillis
litore in hoc steterat (nam stantem in litore vidi),
sentences.l: the woman who a moment ago stood on this shore in cheap clothing, with her hair disordered (for I saw her standing on the shore),
sentences.i: the girl who was standing here on this shore a moment ago in cheap clothes, her hair in disorder — I saw her standing on the shore —
sentences.n: “quae” has no expressed antecedent, “the woman who”, and the whole relative clause is the object of “dic ubi sit” in the next line. “turbatis capillis” is an ablative of description beside “cum vili veste”; the parenthesis sets “stantem in litore” against “litore in hoc steterat”, the man insisting on what he saw.

sentences.t: dic ubi sit: neque enim vestigia longius exstant.”
sentences.l: say where she is: for her tracks stand out no further.”
sentences.i: tell me where she is — her footprints go no further than this.”
sentences.n: “dic ubi sit” is an indirect question and so takes the subjunctive “sit”, where English keeps the indicative. The footprints stop at the water's edge, which is exactly why the question is being put to a man standing in the water; “longius” is the comparative adverb, “further than this point”.

sentences.t:
Illa dei munus bene cedere sensit et a se
se quaeri gaudens, his est resecuta rogantem:
sentences.l: She perceived that the god's gift was turning out well and, rejoicing that she was being sought from herself, answered the questioner with these words:
sentences.i: She saw that the god's gift was working, and, delighted to be asked after herself by herself, answered the questioner so:
sentences.n: “bene cedere” is the idiom for turning out well, and it stands in an accusative and infinitive after “sensit”. “a se se quaeri” sets the same pronoun twice in two cases — that she was being sought from herself — putting the whole joke of the disguise into the grammar; “resecuta est” is the perfect of the deponent “resequor”, active in meaning, “she answered”.

sentences.t:
“Quisquis es, ignoscas; in nullam lumina partem
gurgite ab hoc flexi studioque operatus inhaesi.
sentences.l: “Whoever you are, may you forgive me; I have turned my eyes in no direction away from this pool, and, busied with my pursuit, I have stuck to it.
sentences.i: “Whoever you are, forgive me: I have not turned my eyes anywhere away from this water, but have kept at my work and stayed fixed on it.
sentences.n: “ignoscas” is a jussive subjunctive used as a polite imperative, softer than “ignosce”. “in nullam partem ... flexi” is the Latin for “nowhere”, with “lumina”, “lights”, again standing for eyes as at 801; “operatus” is the participle of the deponent “operor” and is active in sense, a verb used of religious as well as ordinary labour.

sentences.t:
Quoque minus dubites, sic has deus aequoris artes
adiuvet, ut nemo iamdudum litore in isto,
me tamen excepto, nec femina constitit ulla.”
sentences.l: And so that you may doubt the less — so may the god of the sea help this craft of mine, as surely as no one for a long time now has stood on that shore of yours, myself however excepted, nor any woman at all.”
sentences.i: And to leave you in less doubt — as surely as I hope the god of the sea helps my craft, no one has stood on that shore of yours this long while, myself excepted, and no woman at all.”
sentences.n: “Quo ... minus dubites” is a purpose clause with “quo” instead of “ut”, regular where a comparative follows — and this is the “quoque” trap in the flesh: “quō-que”, “and so that”, not the adverb “also”. The oath then runs “sic ... adiuvet ut”, “may the god help me as truly as it is the case that ...”, the same formula begun at 857; “me tamen excepto” is an ablative absolute dropped inside the oath, and it is the exception that keeps every word of it true.

sentences.t:
Credidit et verso dominus pede pressit harenam
elususque abiit: illi sua reddita forma est.
sentences.l: The master believed her and, his foot having been turned, pressed the sand and went off cheated: her own shape was given back to her.
sentences.i: Her master believed her, turned on his heel across the sand and went away deceived; and her own shape was given back to her.
sentences.n: “verso ... pede” is an ablative absolute, “his foot having been turned”, the Latin for turning on one's heel, and “pressit harenam” keeps the footprints of 861 underfoot. “elusus” agrees with “dominus”, from “eludo”, the twin compound of the “delusum” at 826, the cheated throat — the swindle has changed sides.

sentences.t:
Ast ubi habere suam transformia corpora sensit,
saepe pater dominis Triopeida tradit.
sentences.l: But when her father perceived that his own daughter had shape-changing bodies, he often hands the woman of Triopas' line over to masters.
sentences.i: But when her father found that his daughter had a body that could change its shape, again and again he handed the descendant of Triopas over to new masters.
sentences.n: “habere ... corpora” is an accusative and infinitive after “sensit”, with “suam” standing alone for “his own daughter”; “corpora”, plural, is exact — she has one body for each shape. “Triopeida” is a Greek patronymic accusative marking her as of the line of Triopas, as her father was “Triopeius” at 751, and the present “tradit” with “saepe” makes the selling a settled habit rather than an event.

sentences.t:
At illa
nunc equa, nunc ales, modo bos, modo cervus abibat
praebebatque avido non iusta alimenta parenti.
sentences.l: But she would go off now a mare, now a bird, at one time a cow, at another a stag, and kept furnishing unjust nourishment to her greedy father.
sentences.i: But she would get away — now a mare, now a bird, now a cow, now a stag — and kept supplying her greedy father with food come by unjustly.
sentences.n: The four nouns are predicative nominatives with “abibat”, “she went away as a mare”, in the same “nunc ... modo” catalogue that described Proteus at 732–734. “non iusta alimenta” is litotes for food wrongfully got; “avido ... parenti” is the dative with “praebebat”, and the epithet that belongs to the disease has passed to the father.

sentences.t:
Vis tamen illa mali postquam consumpserat omnem
materiam dederatque gravi nova pabula morbo,
sentences.l: But after that force of the evil had used up all the material and had given new fodder to the heavy sickness,
sentences.i: But when the violence of the evil had consumed all its material and had given fresh fodder to that heavy sickness,
sentences.n: “Vis illa mali” is the subject, “that force of the evil”, with “mali” a genitive; “postquam” takes the pluperfect indicative, which English turns into “after it had”. “materiam” is the word for raw stuff and for fuel alike, so the fire-simile of 837 is still burning under the sentence.

sentences.t:
ipse suos artus lacero divellere morsu
coepit et infelix minuendo corpus alebat.
sentences.l: he himself began to tear his own limbs apart with mangling bite, and the wretched man fed his body by diminishing it.
sentences.i: he began to tear his own limbs apart with rending bite, and the wretch fed his body by making it less.
sentences.n: “lacero ... morsu” is an ablative of means, its adjective and noun held apart by “divellere”, “to pull apart”. “minuendo” is a gerund in the ablative of means answering “alebat” — fed by diminishing — so that the punishment ends in the self-cancelling law already stated at 842. Magnus prints “lacero ... morsu”; some editions print “lacerans”, making the participle agree with the man.

sentences.t:
Quid moror externis? Etiam mihi nempe novandi est
corporis, o iuvenis, numero finita potestas.
sentences.l: Why do I linger over other people's affairs? I too, young man, have a power of making my body new, one limited in number.
sentences.i: Why do I dwell on other men's stories? I too, young man, have the power of remaking my body — a power with a fixed number to it.
sentences.n: “externis” is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, “outside matters”, other people's business — the speaker turns from the tale back to himself. “novandi ... corporis” is a gerundive construction depending on “potestas”, and “mihi ... est” is a dative of possession; “numero finita” says the count of his shapes is fixed.

sentences.t:
Nam modo qui nunc sum videor, modo flector in anguem,
armenti modo dux vires in cornua sumo, —
sentences.l: For at one moment I appear as what I now am, at another I am bent into a snake, at another, leader of the herd, I take my strength into my horns —
sentences.i: For one moment I seem what I am now, the next I am twisted into a serpent, the next, as the bull that leads the herd, I gather my strength into my horns —
sentences.n: “qui nunc sum” is a relative clause standing as the complement of “videor”, “I seem to be the thing which I now am”. “flector” is passive in form with a middle force, “I am bent into”, that is “I turn myself into”, and both layers keep the passive shape the Latin uses; “armenti dux” is the bull, named by his office rather than his species, and “vires in cornua sumo” gathers the whole body into the horns that the next line takes away.

sentences.t:
cornua, dum potui! nunc pars caret altera telo
frontis, ut ipse vides.”
sentences.l: horns, while I could! Now the other of the two parts of my forehead lacks its weapon, as you yourself see.”
sentences.i: horns — while I still could! Now one side of my brow has lost its weapon, as you can see for yourself.”
sentences.n: The repeated “cornua” picks the word up from the end of the previous line and turns it against the speaker; “dum potui” is an abrupt elliptical clause, “for as long as I was able”. “caret” takes the ablative “telo”, and “telo frontis”, the weapon of his brow, names the horn as a spear — the line assumes the reader knows how he lost it, and these lines do not narrate it.

sentences.t: Gemitus sunt verba secuti.
sentences.l: Groans followed his words.
sentences.n: “secuti” is masculine plural and so agrees with “gemitus”, the groans, which are therefore the subject and “verba” the object: the groans followed the words, not the other way about. “sequor” is deponent, active in meaning for all its passive form — and “gemitus” is the word given to the wounded oak at 758, returned here to the teller of the tale.
